title: Salt in the Water
hook: a father drops salt into water overnight and tells his son, "you are that", and three great teachers hear it three ways
carry: tat tvam asi: three great readings, none ranked
tomorrow: a dead teacher's hand has three fingers folded. what did he leave undone?

segments.voice: Yesterday in Vedanta, Bhrigu climbed from food to bliss: Brahman, where everything comes from, lives in, and returns to.

Back to Shvetaketu and his father. Uddalaka hands him a lump of salt. Put this in a cup of water, he says, and bring it to me in the morning. Next morning: give me the salt. Shvetaketu looks. It's gone. Taste the water from the top. Salty. From the middle. Salty. From the bottom. Salty. You can't see it, his father says, but it's there, all through. That finest essence is the self of all this. That is the real. That is the self. You are that, Shvetaketu. In Sanskrit, tat tvam asi.
screen: `SALT IN THE WATER OVERNIGHT.` → `GONE, YET SALTY EVERYWHERE.` → `TAT TVAM ASI. YOU ARE THAT.`

segments.voice: Tat tvam asi is one of the most loved lines in Hinduism, and here's the teaching inside it: your atman, your deepest self, is not cut off from Brahman. But how? Three of Vedanta's great teachers honor this same line and hear it differently. Shankara reads it straight. You, at your deepest, are Brahman, not part of it. Advaita teachers use the space inside a clay pot: break the pot, and the space was never separate. His school is Advaita, not-two. Ramanuja keeps the self real. In another Upanishad, the sage Yajnavalkya speaks of the one who dwells within all things, whose body they are, who guides them from inside. So for Ramanuja, the world and every self are like Brahman's body: truly real, never apart. You are that, the way a body belongs to the one who lives in it. His school is Vishishtadvaita. Madhva hears difference. For him, the Lord, whom he knows as Vishnu, and the self are always two, and the self depends on him completely, like a reflection that's real only because something shines. His school is Dvaita, two. Three readings, each argued from the same words, and Hindus in each line live and pray by them today. None is ranked here. What all three share is the salt: the self is never on its own, outside the sacred.
screen: `ATMAN AND BRAHMAN.` · `SHANKARA: NEVER TWO.` · `RAMANUJA: THE WORLD AS GOD'S BODY.` · `MADHVA: ALWAYS TWO, ALWAYS CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Let the words come quietly, you are that. Hear them first as Shankara might, as open space no pot ever divided. Then as Ramanuja might, held from inside, the way a body belongs to the one who lives in it. Then as Madhva might, noticing you didn't make yourself shine. A few breaths each. You don't have to choose. If you pray, you can let the line rest in the name you pray to.
Vedanta. Today, the line you are that, heard as not-two, as body and soul, and as two who stay close. Today's word.
Your line: tat tvam asi, three great readings, none ranked. Like salt in water, the self is never outside the sacred. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Hindus in the Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita lines each study the Upanishads through their own teacher's commentary, Shankara's, Ramanuja's or Madhva's, and the line tat tvam asi is read and taught in each lineage in its own way.

original.note: Sanskrit: you are that, from the Chandogya Upanishad, read differently by each Vedanta school.

trapdoor: what you thought: tat tvam asi means Hindus think they're God.
what it means: the self is never outside the sacred, and the great Vedanta teachers read that as not-two, as body and soul, or as two who stay close.

what a scholar hears: Chandogya 6.13 (the salt) inside the tat tvam asi refrain of 6.8-6.16, read by Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita, with Ramanuja leaning on the inner controller of Brihadaranyaka 3.7.

Tat tvam asi.meaning: you are that: a father's teaching in the Chandogya Upanishad

Vishishtadvaita.meaning: Ramanuja's school: the world and selves as Brahman's body

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.13 (the salt in water; tasting from top, middle and bottom; you are that)
Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7–6.16 (Uddalaka to Shvetaketu: the refrain, you are that)
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.7 (the inner controller, whose body all things are)
Shankara, Ramanuja and Madhva on Chandogya 6.8.7 and on the Brahma Sutra

notes: The pot-space image (ghatakasha) is standard in Advaita teaching; confirm it fits Shankara rather than only later Advaita.
Ramanuja's body-soul reading (sharira-shariri bhava) and use of Brihadaranyaka 3.7: confirm.

Madhva's reading: the script says only that he hears closeness and likeness, never sameness, and uses the reflection image (pratibimba). Some in his line read the sandhi as 'atat tvam asi'; deliberately left out. A Dvaita Keeper should check the framing.
The salt and seed teachings in Chandogya 6 are paraphrased and ordered loosely; confirm.
